to be hung; hang, of an object
to spend time; get along; be doing
for a fire to break out

go in; enter away from the speaker
Long time no see; it has been a while
I am doing well; are you doing well?

You are all right, aren't you? respectful
what number, how many, which numeric value
how much, how many in a broader quantity sense
to; for; sometimes from a person or animal
at; in (location of an action); from
to/from a person (depending on the verb)
to/from a person (depending on the verb)

firebox of a traditional stove or heating system
uncle (a family term; exact use depends on the relationship)

It is normal; it is average

cards.kr: 겨울은 보통 추워요. 하지만 오늘은 안 추워요.
cards.en: Winter is usually cold. But today it is not cold.
What did you do on the weekend?
I am resting at home because I am tired.
I am staying home because of the weather.
We ate the food we brought together.
I want to go to Korea.
It is a shirt made of silk.
I go to work by bus.
I eat a meal. Then I drink coffee.
The fruit is fresh and sweet.
There is a toilet and a bathtub.
I ate lunch with a friend.
When I go home, I eat.
I wash my hands before sleeping.
A restaurant is a place where people eat.
I wash my face in the bathroom.
I get up in the morning.
Because the window is big, sunlight comes in well.
I sit down and draw a picture.
Teacher, how have you been recently?
There is a television in front of the sofa.
As for the bathroom, there is a washbasin.
It is thundering and there is lightning.
What is the weather like today? It is clear.
I turn off the light when I go to bed.
The door is heavy but opens easily.
A sound is coming from outside.
I close the window because of the rain.
I go to the library every Saturday.
The weather is not good today.

cards.kr: 창문을 닫았어요. 왜냐하면 비가 오기 때문이에요.
cards.en: I closed the window because it is raining.
The room is full of sunlight.
The room is bright because the window is large.
There is no key; I do not have a key.
I read a book when I want to rest.
I give a book to a friend.
I received a book from a friend.
This book is important to me.

cards.kr: 일 안 할 때 책을 읽어요.
cards.en: I read a book when I am not working.
I take a walk with a friend.
I eat dumplings in the evening.
I stay home because of the rain.
I am trying to do better.
I read a book at home yesterday.
I give a book to a friend.
I invite a friend to dinner.
What kind of food is it?
I make dumplings for a friend.
I receive money from the company.
Slice the onion. Then sauté it.
Add the sauce when the meat is cooked.
Repeat until the dish is full.
The book is inside the bag.

patterns.explanation: Attach -아요 after a stem whose last vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ, otherwise -어요; 하다 becomes 해요. Common contractions and irregular forms must be learned with each verb. This form can describe a present action, habit or state.
A polite sentence can become a question with questioning intonation and context. Korean often keeps the same word order.

patterns.en: Go or come to a place
patterns.explanation: 에 marks a destination with 가다 or 오다. Replace 어디 with a place to answer a where-question.

examples.en: I am going to a cafe.

patterns.explanation: With 오다, 에서 can mark the place of origin. It also has a separate action-location use.

patterns.en: Ask what someone does, eats or drinks
patterns.explanation: Put 뭐 in the object position and use the appropriate conjugated verb. The answer replaces 뭐 with the thing.
Add the past ending to a verb or adjective stem: -았어요 with ㅏ/ㅗ stems, otherwise -었어요; 하다 becomes 했어요. Learn contractions such as 가다 → 갔어요 and 보다 → 봤어요.

examples.en: I was busy on the weekend.

patterns.explanation: Use -ㄹ 거예요 after a vowel stem and -을 거예요 after most consonant stems. A stem already ending in ㄹ keeps that ㄹ. The exact meaning may be a plan or a prediction.

examples.en: I am going to eat pasta this evening.

patterns.explanation: Place 안 before the conjugated verb or adjective. With separable noun + 하다 verbs, use noun + 안 해요, such as 공부 안 해요.

examples.en: I am not busy these days.

patterns.explanation: 그리고 starts another related sentence and can also connect nouns in simple speech.
하지만 introduces a contrasting statement. It can combine a usual situation with an exception.

examples.ko: 겨울은 보통 추워요. 하지만 오늘은 안 추워요.
examples.en: Winter is usually cold. But today it is not cold.

patterns.explanation: Use 항상 for always, 보통 for usually, 자주 for often and 가끔 for sometimes. These words do not impose fixed numerical frequencies.
절대 needs a negative expression to mean never. The learned form places 안 before the verb.
In 듣다, final ㄷ changes to ㄹ before a vowel-starting ending. This is an irregular pattern; not every ㄷ-ending verb changes.

patterns.en: At, in or on a time
patterns.explanation: Use 에 with words such as 아침, 점심, 저녁, 밤, 주말 and weekdays. 어제, 오늘, 내일 and 지금 normally stand alone without 에.
아침, 점심 and 저녁 can name either a time of day or its meal. 에 marks the time; without it, the word can be the meal being eaten.

patterns.en: Say what someone or something is
patterns.explanation: Use 이에요 after a consonant-ending noun and 예요 after a vowel-ending noun. The noun with 은/는 is the topic.
아니에요 is the polite form of 아니다. Use 이 after a consonant and 가 after a vowel on the noun being negated; do not write 안이에요.

patterns.en: Make and negate noun + do verbs
patterns.explanation: Some activity nouns combine with 하다, such as 공부하다, 청소하다 and 연습하다. In the practiced negative form, put 안 before 하다: 연습 안 해요.
Use 은 after a consonant and 는 after a vowel. It presents what the sentence is about and can signal a contrast. It does not always mean a universal or general fact.

examples.en: As for the coffee, it is delicious.

patterns.explanation: Use 이 after a consonant and 가 after a vowel. This identifies the subject and can focus attention on new or selected information. Both topic and subject choices depend on context.
Use 을 after a consonant and 를 after a vowel to mark the thing acted on. Spoken Korean can omit a clear particle, but keep it in these practice sentences.
Place 의 between the owner and the owned noun. 저의 contracts to 제 in humble speech.
들 can mark plurality. Korean nouns can also refer to more than one thing without 들; the adjective does not change for plural agreement.
있어요 describes existence or possession. It is present-style, not a past ending; the past form is 있었어요.

examples.en: There is a box in the living room.

patterns.explanation: 맛있다 means delicious and 재미있다 means interesting or fun. Their forms include 있어요, but are not past tense: 맛있어요 is present-style; 맛있었어요 is past.

patterns.en: Put a description before a noun
patterns.explanation: For the practiced regular forms, use ㄴ after a vowel stem and 은 after a consonant stem: 큰 집, 작은 가방. ㄹ stems drop ㄹ before ㄴ, as in 길다 → 긴. 있다/없다 compounds use -는: 맛있는. These are descriptions, not independent sentences.

patterns.en: This, that and that over there
patterns.explanation: 이 is near the speaker; 그 is near the listener or something already mentioned or shared in context; 저 is visibly distant from both.

examples.en: That house over there is big.

patterns.en: This one, that one and that one over there
patterns.explanation: These stand alone, unlike 이/그/저 before a noun. Use 뭐예요? to ask what a thing is.

patterns.en: Set a time as a topic or contrast
patterns.explanation: Adding 은/는 can emphasize a time or contrast it with another time. The contrast is contextual; it does not automatically mean that an action is unusual.
에 marks the location with 있어요. This states where someone or something is; it does not imply they are doing nothing.

examples.en: The book is in the room.

patterns.explanation: Use 에서 for the place where an action takes place, such as studying, eating or working.

examples.en: I read a book in the library.

patterns.explanation: 도 adds another item to the statement. In these examples it replaces 이/가 or 은/는 and can also replace an object particle.
정말 emphasizes a description as really or truly. 너무 can mean too or, in everyday speech, very, depending on context.
Use 뭐 했어요? with a time expression to ask what someone did. Future practice uses 뭐 할 거예요?

examples.en: What did you do on the weekend?

patterns.explanation: 왜냐하면 introduces an explanation, meaning because or the reason is. The lessons practiced it before a simple polite reason sentence.

examples.en: I am resting at home because I am tired.

patterns.explanation: Attach 때문에 to a noun or noun phrase naming the cause, then give the result. Do not attach it directly to a bare verb stem.

examples.en: I am staying home because of the weather.

patterns.explanation: Place 잘 before a verb to describe doing the action well, as in 잘 쉬었어요.

At a pause or before another consonant, Korean final consonants are realized using seven basic sound categories: ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ. Following sounds can change pronunciation, so read the whole word.

examples.en: clothes: final ㅅ is pronounced as an unreleased t sound
front: final ㅍ is pronounced as an unreleased p sound

patterns.explanation: ㅊ has a stronger puff of air than ㅈ. 추웠어요 means it was cold; 주웠어요 means picked something up. Also distinguish the tense initial ㄸ in 딸 from ㄷ in 달.
님 adds respect to a title. Learn complete established forms such as 선생님 and 어머님; forms of address depend on the relationship and context.

patterns.pattern: 학 / 년 / 내 in related words
patterns.explanation: The lesson introduced 학 as study/learning in 학생, 학년 and 대학; 년 means year in 작년 and 내년. This helps recognize related words, but similar-sounding syllables are not always the same root.
힘 means strength or energy, and 나다 means arise or come out. The expression 힘이 나다 means to feel strength or energy returning.
마다 attaches to a noun, including a time unit, place or thing. It indicates each instance.
Use the 아/어 form plus 주다 to show that an action benefits someone. The lesson practiced 도와주다, 사주다 and 써 주다.

examples.en: I wrote a letter for someone.
I buy coffee for a friend.

patterns.en: Describe something through a completed action
patterns.explanation: With an action verb, -(으)ㄴ before a noun commonly describes a completed action: 가져온 음식 is the food someone brought. This differs from the present descriptive-adjective use of -(으)ㄴ.

examples.en: We ate the food we brought together.

patterns.explanation: 열심히 means diligently or with effort; 조금 means a little. They describe different aspects of the action rather than being exact opposites.

patterns.en: Keep ㅎ distinct from no initial consonant
patterns.explanation: 안 begins with a vowel; 회사 begins with ㅎ. Do not add an h sound to 안, 아침 or 오늘. Pronounce the written ㅎ in words such as 회사 and 헬스장 naturally without an exaggerated puff.
Attach 고 싶어요 to the verb stem, not to its polite form. This expresses the speaker’s wish, or asks about the listener’s wish.

examples.en: I want to go to Korea.

patterns.explanation: Attach 고 있어요 to an action-verb stem for an action in progress.
Use ㄹ 수 after a vowel-ending stem and 을 수 after most consonant-ending stems. A ㄹ-ending stem takes 수 directly: 만들 수 있어요.
Use 로 after a vowel or ㄹ, and 으로 after other consonants. This highlights direction; 에 marks the destination. An additional purpose is not required.

patterns.en: make with a material; made of
patterns.explanation: Use (으)로 for an ingredient or material. The lesson used 만든 as a fixed modifier meaning made.

examples.en: It is a shirt made of silk.
I make a cake with blueberries.

patterns.explanation: Use (으)로 to mark a means of transport, a tool, or the language used.

examples.en: I go to work by bus.
I go to work by car.

patterns.en: find the verb or adjective stem
patterns.explanation: Remove 다 from the dictionary form before choosing an ending. 가다 → 가-, 먹다 → 먹-, 마시다 → 마시-. Some endings require a sound change.

examples.en: To go → I want to go.

patterns.explanation: Attach 자 to a verb stem for a casual suggestion with friends or peers. This is not a polite ending.

patterns.pattern: 오늘 / 어제 / 내일 / 지금 / 방금 + sentence
patterns.explanation: These everyday time expressions usually function without time-marker 에. They can still take topic or contrast particles, as in 오늘은.
은/는 frames a topic or contrast; 이/가 identifies the subject. The choice depends on context, not a strict general-versus-specific rule. Use 은/이 after consonants and 는/가 after vowels.

examples.en: As for today, the weather is good.

patterns.pattern: 비가 와요 / 눈이 와요 / 우박이 와요
patterns.explanation: Korean commonly describes rain, snow, and hail with 오다, literally come. Use 비가, 눈이, and 우박이 with the appropriate subject particle.
그리고 links a new sentence to the previous one by adding another action or piece of information.

examples.en: I eat a meal. Then I drink coffee.

patterns.explanation: Attach 고 to a verb or adjective stem to connect actions or descriptions. The final predicate carries the polite ending and often the overall tense.

examples.en: The fruit is fresh and sweet.
There is a desk and also a wardrobe.
I hold the handle and turn it.

patterns.explanation: 하고 connects nouns or marks a companion in ordinary spoken Korean. Context distinguishes and from with; it does not by itself determine the politeness of the sentence.
Use 이랑 after a consonant and 랑 after a vowel. It connects nouns or indicates someone doing an action together.

examples.en: There is a toilet and a bathtub.

patterns.en: and; with, often written or formal
patterns.explanation: Use 와 after a vowel and 과 after a consonant. It has the same basic linking functions as 하고 and (이)랑, with register differences.

examples.en: I ate lunch with a friend.
There are a book and a pen.

patterns.explanation: 식사하다 is a more formal lexical choice than 밥 먹다. Both examples use polite 요; neither is casual banmal.
우리 is common with home and family, even when English uses my. 제 집 is also grammatical when individual possession matters.
Use 면 after a vowel or ㄹ, and 으면 after other consonants. It sets a condition or a recurring when situation.

examples.en: When I go home, I eat.
When the room is clean, I feel good.
The door closes when the wind blows.

patterns.explanation: Attach 기 전에 to the verb stem. 자기 전에 is 자- from 자다 plus 기 전에; 자기 here does not mean oneself.

examples.en: I wash my hands before sleeping.
I wash my hands before eating.

patterns.en: it is a place where one does something
patterns.explanation: Use an action-verb stem plus 는 before 곳 to describe a place by an action done there.

examples.en: A restaurant is a place where people eat.

patterns.pattern: 하나 / 한 개, 두 개, 세 개
patterns.explanation: Native number 하나 becomes 한 before a counter. 개 is a general counter. Both 하나 있어요 and 한 개 있어요 are possible; two and three become 두 and 세 before a counter.
에서 marks where an action happens, unlike 에 with 있어요, which locates something. 여기에서 can contract to 여기서; this is not a rule that every 에서 can shorten to 서.

examples.en: I wash my face in the bathroom.
I read a book at the library.

patterns.explanation: Place an event or time noun before 전에. For an action verb, first use 기 to make an action noun.

patterns.en: turn an action into a noun-like form
patterns.explanation: 기 attaches to a verb stem to create a noun-like action expression, as in 읽기 or 자기. The lesson analyzed this inside 자기 전에.
또 comes before a predicate to express repetition or an additional action.
Time expressions and adverbs add context to a core sentence. Time often appears early, and the main predicate normally remains last.

examples.en: I get up in the morning.
I am a little busy these days.

patterns.explanation: Korean commonly places the predicate last. Particles allow some earlier phrases to change order for emphasis; one sentence can contain several clauses, not only one verb.

examples.en: As for the coffee, I drink it.
I read a book at home in the morning.

patterns.explanation: This ending connects a reason or cause to its result. 크다 becomes 커서 and 하다 becomes 해서.

examples.en: Because the window is big, sunlight comes in well.
I am full because I ate a meal.
I go outside because the weather is nice.

patterns.en: do an action and then continue
patterns.explanation: This ending also links closely connected actions. 앉아서 그림을 그려요 describes sitting down and drawing while seated.

examples.en: I sit down and draw a picture.

patterns.explanation: These established Sino-Korean time words express regular frequency. They are normal in everyday speech as well as writing.

examples.en: I read a book every day.

patterns.explanation: Intonation makes 잘 지내요 a statement or a question. 잘 지내세요? is a respectful question; the subject is usually understood.

patterns.pattern: Omit you or use a title
patterns.explanation: When asking back, Korean often repeats or varies the question without a direct you pronoun. A title such as 선생님 can be used when appropriate.

examples.en: Teacher, how have you been recently?

patterns.explanation: 더 adds comparative degree or additional quantity. It means more, not the superlative most.

patterns.en: at a time; to a destination; at a place
patterns.explanation: 에 marks many times, a destination with motion verbs, or the location of existence. Repeated 에 in 아침에 회사에 가요 is normal. 에 is normally omitted with 오늘, 어제, 내일, 지금, and 방금.

examples.en: I went to the garden on Saturday.

patterns.en: in front of, beside, on, inside
patterns.explanation: Combine an object with a location noun such as 앞, 옆, 위, 밑, 아래, 안, 밖, or 가운데, then 에. The object belongs inside that location phrase. Context distinguishes on from above; 안에 makes the inside relationship explicit. 밖에 나가요 means go outside.

examples.en: There is a television in front of the sofa.
There is a book on the desk.
There is a book inside the box.

patterns.en: attach the particle to the whole noun
patterns.explanation: A compound such as 가족사진 is treated as one noun, so the subject particle follows the complete word.

patterns.en: hang something; be hung; be hanging
patterns.explanation: 걸다 takes the thing hung as an object. 걸리다 makes that thing the subject; 걸려 있어요 describes the resulting hanging state. This is one specific passive pair.

examples.en: A photo is hanging on the wall.

patterns.en: as for at/in that place or time
patterns.explanation: 에 plus 는 sets a location or time as a topic and can suggest a contrast. It does not inherently mean only in that place.

examples.en: As for the bathroom, there is a washbasin.

patterns.explanation: Noun identity uses 이에요 after a consonant or 예요 after a vowel. Descriptive adjectives conjugate directly, as 깨끗해요. Existence or location uses 있어요.

patterns.en: saying a color using a noun
patterns.explanation: 흰색 and 검은색 are color nouns ending in a consonant, so use 이에요. Compare the adjective predicate 까매요.
천둥 and 번개 commonly pair with 치다 rather than the precipitation expression 오다.

examples.en: It is thundering and there is lightning.

patterns.explanation: 어때요 asks what something is like. A weather answer can use a descriptive word or a weather-event expression.

examples.en: What is the weather like today? It is clear.

patterns.explanation: 나 is non-humble I and 저 is humble I. 내 and 제 mean my; 내가 and 제가 are subject-marked forms. Polite speech usually pairs 저는 with 제.
-들 follows a noun to make plurality explicit. Korean often leaves number to context; verbs do not change to agree with singular or plural nouns. A case particle can follow -들.

patterns.en: Coming in, going in, going out
patterns.explanation: 들어오다 describes entering toward the speaker or viewpoint; 들어가다 describes going inside, and 나가다 going outside. 들어 in these verbs is not the plural suffix -들.

patterns.en: Like something versus something is good
patterns.explanation: 좋아하다 takes the liked thing as an object marked 을/를. 좋다 is descriptive and normally uses 이/가 for the thing that is good or liked in context.
Start with the dictionary stem. Add -ㄹ 때 after a vowel and -을 때 after most consonants; an existing final ㄹ is retained. Examples include 잘 때, 들어갈 때, 닫을 때, and 일할 때.

examples.en: I turn off the light when I go to bed.
I drink water when I work.

patterns.explanation: Attach -지만 to the stem to contrast two statements. The final clause carries the sentence ending.

examples.en: The door is heavy but opens easily.

patterns.en: A sound occurs or comes from somewhere
patterns.explanation: 나다 describes a sound arising or being produced. It does not mean that someone deliberately makes the sound.

examples.en: A sound is coming from outside.

patterns.en: because of; it is because of
patterns.explanation: N 때문에 connects a cause noun to a following result in the same sentence. N 때문이에요 ends a sentence naming the cause. Verbal cause clauses use forms such as -아서/어서 or -기 때문에.

examples.en: I close the window because of the rain.
The street is wet. It is because of the rain.

patterns.explanation: 매주 plus a weekday identifies a recurring weekly event. Contrast 이번 주 for this week only.

examples.en: I go to the library every Saturday.

patterns.explanation: Attach -지 않아요 to the stem. It is an alternative to short 안 negation; register and emphasis depend on context rather than a strict formal-versus-casual rule.

examples.en: The weather is not good today.

patterns.explanation: 왜냐하면 introduces a reason after a statement or question. A complete reason sentence often ends in -(기) 때문이에요; it is not just a replacement for every English because.

examples.ko: 창문을 닫았어요. 왜냐하면 비가 오기 때문이에요.
examples.en: I closed the window because it is raining.

patterns.explanation: Use 로 after a vowel or ㄹ and 으로 after other consonants. With 가득하다, the phrase identifies what fills the space.

examples.en: The room is full of sunlight.
The box is full of books.

patterns.explanation: Attach -기 때문에 to a predicate stem to make it a cause clause. The reason usually precedes the result; 있다 becomes 있기 때문에.

examples.en: The room is bright because the window is large.

patterns.explanation: 없다 is the ordinary absence/not-have counterpart of 있다, and 모르다 means not know. 좋다, 안 좋다, and 싫다 express different evaluations; dislike is not always as strong as hate.

examples.en: There is no key; I do not have a key.
I do not know that name.

patterns.en: when one wants to do something
patterns.explanation: Attach -고 싶다 to an action stem. Adding -(으)ㄹ 때 to 싶다 gives 싶을 때. First-person examples avoid overgeneralizing -고 싶다 to claims about another person’s unobserved feelings.

examples.en: I read a book when I want to rest.

patterns.en: This, that, and that over there
patterns.explanation: 이- usually refers near the speaker; 그- can refer near the listener or to something already mentioned; 저- points to something distant from both. Visibility is a useful cue, not an absolute rule.

patterns.en: Look at something versus something is visible
patterns.explanation: 보다 takes the thing seen or watched as an object. 보이다 in the visibility sense takes the visible thing as subject. Deliberate watching often uses 보다, but intention alone is not an absolute distinction.

examples.en: The sky is visible; I can see the sky.

patterns.explanation: 의 links a noun to another noun, often as possession. In ordinary speech the particle 의 may be pronounced 에; spelling remains 의. It can be omitted in some familiar noun combinations.
에게 and conversational 한테 mark a person or animal related to the action, often the recipient. 을/를 separately marks the direct object.

examples.en: I give a book to a friend.
I put a harness on the cat.

patterns.explanation: With 받다, 에게 or 한테 may identify the source and translate as from. 에게서 explicitly marks a personal source; the verb and context determine the role.

examples.en: I received a book from a friend.

patterns.explanation: 에게 can identify the person for whom a statement holds. This is a separate use from a recipient in a giving sentence.

examples.en: This book is important to me.

patterns.en: What is cleaned versus where cleaning happens
patterns.explanation: An object marker names what is cleaned; 에서 names where the action occurs. A location-only sentence can leave the cleaned object implicit.

examples.en: I cleaned the desk at home.

patterns.pattern: N 안 할 때 / N 안 했어요
patterns.explanation: With common noun-plus-하다 activity verbs, 안 often appears before 하다. Use the stem 하-, not the polite form 해요, when building 할 때.

examples.ko: 일 안 할 때 책을 읽어요.
examples.en: I read a book when I am not working.

patterns.explanation: 아무거나 expresses free choice: anything or any one. 아무것도 normally combines with a negative predicate such as 안 먹어요 or 없어요 to mean not anything/nothing.

examples.en: There is nothing in the box.

patterns.en: Opening or closing something versus it opening or closing
patterns.explanation: 열다 and 닫다 take the thing acted on as object; 열리다 and 닫히다 make the door/window the subject. 닫혔어요 reports that it closed or was closed; a continuing closed state is more explicitly 닫혀 있어요.

examples.en: The door closed; the door was closed.

patterns.explanation: Write dates from the largest unit to the smallest. Years, months and dates use Sino-Korean numbers.
These connect nouns or mark a companion. Use 이랑/과 after a consonant and 랑/와 after a vowel. 하고 works after either.

examples.en: I take a walk with a friend.
There are a book and a notebook.

patterns.explanation: Some activity nouns combine with 하다. The object particle can be omitted in many everyday expressions.
물을 주다 means to give water. 에 marks the recipient or destination, such as a garden.
Use an adjective modifier before the noun, then the past copula. After a consonant use 이었어요; after a vowel use 였어요.
Combine 오늘 with 아침에 to say this morning. 오늘 alone does not take 에 in this use.
Place 동안 after a duration to say how long an action or state lasts.
Use the verb stem plus -고 나서 to show that the first action finishes before the next one.
나다 appears in expressions for an event or phenomenon occurring, such as 불이 나다. It is different from merely saying something exists.
좋아요 completes a sentence, 좋은 describes a noun, and 좋게 describes how an action is done. These forms have different jobs.
저녁 can mean evening or dinner. 에 marks the time; 으로 can mark the meal something is eaten for.

examples.en: I eat dumplings in the evening.

patterns.explanation: Attach -는 동안 to an action verb stem to describe an action happening during another action.
좋아하는 modifies the noun. 가장 adds the meaning most; finish the sentence with the thing you choose.
Use 때문에 after a noun and -기 때문에 after a verb or adjective stem. The reason comes before the result in these sentences.

examples.en: I stay home because of the rain.
I stay home because I am busy.

patterns.explanation: These can refer back to the subject as an object. Their natural use depends on context; 스스로 also emphasizes doing something oneself.
Turn an action into a noun-like phrase with -는 것, then mark it as the object of 좋아해요.
Use -는 것이 before 그리워요 to say that you miss an activity or experience.
Attach -(으)려고 해요 to a verb stem to express intention or an attempt. It is not a general substitute for every English use of try.

examples.en: I am trying to do better.

patterns.explanation: Use 후에 after a noun, or -(으)ㄴ 후에 after an action verb, to place the next action after it.

examples.en: I sleep after watching a movie.

patterns.explanation: Place the final action or description at the end. Begin with a short sentence, then add time, place or reasons.

examples.en: I read a book at home yesterday.

patterns.explanation: 이/가 marks the subject in these examples; 을/를 marks the object affected by or associated with the action.
Korean often leaves the subject unstated when it is clear from context. Keep it when omission would cause confusion.
State the purpose with -(으)러 before a motion verb such as 가다. Add 으러 after most consonants and 러 after vowels or ㄹ.
These mark a person connected with giving or receiving. The verb helps determine to versus from. 한테 is common in conversation; 에게 is neutral and common in writing.

examples.en: I give a book to a friend.
I receive a book from a friend.

patterns.explanation: 에 can mark the event or occasion that someone is invited to.

examples.en: I invite a friend to dinner.

patterns.explanation: Use 이에요 after consonants and 예요 after vowels. The past forms are 이었어요 and 였어요. 이예요 is not the standard spelling.
Stems whose final vowel is ㅏ or ㅗ usually take 아요; other vowels usually take 어요. 하다 becomes 해요. Contractions and irregular verbs need individual practice.
보다 after a noun gives the reference point for a comparison.
Use these descriptions when quantity is the main point, rather than translating every English there is literally with 있어요.
Use 이/가 before 되다 for what someone or something becomes.
-고 싶어요 expresses a desire to do something. -(으)면 좋겠어요 expresses a wish for a situation to happen.
끝나다 describes something ending. 끝내다 describes someone finishing a task and can take an object.
언제 asks about time broadly. An answer may be a day, a part of the day or a more exact time.
몇 asks for a numerical answer. Keep the appropriate counter or unit, such as 개, 시 or 월.
무슨 asks for the type or identity of a thing.

examples.en: What kind of food is it?

patterns.explanation: Use this for the benefit of someone or something. It is different from every English use of for.

examples.en: I make dumplings for a friend.

patterns.explanation: 에서 can mark an organization or other source with 받다.

examples.en: I receive money from the company.

patterns.explanation: Use this to move to the next step after the previous one. 그때 instead means at that time.

examples.en: Slice the onion. Then sauté it.

patterns.en: When doing; when something has happened
patterns.explanation: Attach the time clause to the event that supplies the condition, then put the main action afterward.

examples.en: Add the sauce when the meat is cooked.

patterns.explanation: 익다 describes the food becoming cooked. 익히다 describes cooking the food.
때까지 can describe the point up to which an action continues.

examples.en: Repeat until the dish is full.

patterns.explanation: 부터 marks the beginning of a period or sequence.
안 means inside. Add 에 when marking a static location.

examples.en: The book is inside the bag.

patterns.en: A person associated with an activity
patterns.explanation: -꾼 occurs in words for a person associated with an activity. Learn established words such as 이야기꾼 rather than adding it freely to every noun.
In the learned word 만족스럽다, the ending creates a descriptive verb meaning satisfying. This word-building ending is not freely usable with every noun.
The lesson introduced a weather-report chunk with -다고 했어요. Use 비가 온다고 했어요 as the reviewed model; wider indirect-speech forms need separate practice.
